summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client ask the server to deliver a message within a set period of time. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When you mail a letter you can ask that it arrive by a certain day. This lets email senders ask that too.

subtitle: How an email sender can ask a mail server to deliver by a deadline, and say what should happen if the deadline is missed.

tldr.problem: Normally a sender has no way to say that a message is only useful if it arrives within a certain time, or to ask to be told early about delays.
tldr.mechanism: The Deliver By extension adds a BY parameter to the SMTP MAIL FROM command. It gives a number of seconds and a mode: R to return the message as undeliverable, or N to send a delayed notification and keep trying.
tldr.outcome: Servers are not required to give such messages any special priority, so the sender gets a statement of intent and clearer failure reporting, not faster delivery.

today: RFC 2852 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000 and its metadata lists no obsoleting RFC. It updates RFC 1894 by adding the Deliver-by-date DSN field.

sections.title: What Deliver By Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2852 defines a way for an SMTP client to ask a server to deliver a message within a prescribed period. The client also says what to do if that does not happen: return the message as undeliverable with no further processing, or issue a delayed delivery status notification (DSN) and keep trying.

The RFC gives two typical uses. A sender may not want a page delivered after business hours, so the message is marked so that delivery attempts stop at 17:00. Or a sender may want a warning if a message is not delivered within, say, 30 minutes, while delivery attempts continue.

This is not a priority mechanism. A receiving server may give a Deliver By message whatever processing priority it likes. The request expresses urgency and makes processing more predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing 'must arrive by 5 o'clock' on a package. You can ask for it to be thrown away if it is late, or for someone to tell you it is late while it keeps travelling.

sections.title: Advertising the Extension
sections.content:
Deliver By uses the SMTP service extension mechanism. The extension is named Deliver By and its EHLO keyword is DELIVERBY. A client sends EHLO, and if the server answers with code 250 and lists DELIVERBY, the extension is supported. No new SMTP verbs are defined.

The keyword may carry one optional parameter, a min-by-time: the smallest by-time the server will accept when the mode is R. A client that asks for mode R with a by-time strictly below that limit is rejected with a permanent failure (55z) reply. If the parameter is left out, nothing is said about a minimum.

The extension also lengthens the maximum MAIL FROM command line by 17 characters to make room for the BY keyword and value.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells the sender up front, 'I understand deadlines, but I will not take a deadline shorter than this many seconds.'

sections.title: The BY Parameter on MAIL FROM
sections.content:
The extended MAIL FROM command is the usual command plus BY= and a value of the form by-time;by-mode, optionally followed by a trace letter. The pieces are:

  • by-time: a decimal number of seconds within which to deliver, from -999,999,999 to +999,999,999 (about 31.6 years either way).
  • by-mode: N (Notify) or R (Return).
  • by-trace: the optional letter T, which asks for tracing.

The by-time is a delta, not a clock time. This avoids trouble from clocks that disagree between client and server. The server adds the by-time to its own current time to get a deliver-by-time. Network delay slightly stretches the effective time, more so with each hop. A by-time does not extend the normal retention period of the server, and it is not a 'deliver after' time.

With mode N, zero or negative values are allowed and are not an error: they record that the deadline already passed. With mode R, zero or negative is a syntax error and the server SHOULD answer 501 (enhanced code 5.5.4 if supported). If a valid request cannot be honored for a server-specific reason, the server SHOULD answer 455 if the condition is transient or 555 if permanent.
sections.plainLanguage: You write 'in 120 seconds' rather than 'at 3:02 PM,' because your clock and the post office's clock might not agree. Then you add R for 'send it back' or N for 'just tell me.'

sections.title: What the Server Does With a Deadline
sections.content:
If the message is delivered before the deliver-by-time, nothing special happens, except that a 'delivered' DSN is returned if the DSN extension is supported and NOTIFY included SUCCESS.

If delivery fails for a temporary reason before the deadline, the server continues to try according to local policy. If it fails for a permanent reason before the deadline, the server MUST return a 'failed' DSN to each recipient with no NOTIFY parameter or with NOTIFY including FAILURE.

When the deadline passes, the mode matters:

  • R: no further delivery attempts may be made, and the server MUST issue a 'failed' DSN with status 5.4.7 ('delivery time expired').
  • N: attempts continue under local policy, and the server MUST issue a 'delayed' DSN with status 4.4.7 ('delivery time expired'), for recipients with no NOTIFY parameter or NOTIFY including DELAY.

A server whose normal retention period is shorter than the by-time MAY still return the message as undeliverable early.
sections.plainLanguage: If the package is late and you said 'send it back,' the post office stops and returns it. If you said 'just tell me,' it sends you a note and keeps trying.

sections.title: Relaying and MX Hosts
sections.content:
When a message with a Deliver By request is passed on to another SMTP server that supports the extension, a new BY parameter MUST be sent with the number of seconds left until the deliver-by-time, computed as close to sending as is reasonable. For mode N this can be negative.

Mode R is strict: the message MUST NOT be relayed to a server without Deliver By support, and the next server's minimum by-time MUST NOT exceed the time left. If it cannot be relayed, it is treated as permanently undeliverable. Mode N may be relayed to any server, but if the next server lacks the extension the relaying client MUST issue a 'relayed' DSN, and SHOULD request NOTIFY with DELAY if the next server supports DSNs. If the trace letter T is used, a 'relayed' DSN SHOULD be generated at each relay.

Sites that route mail through MX records need all their MX hosts to support Deliver By, and clients SHOULD NOT try multiple MX hosts looking for one that does. MX hosts should choose their min-by-time carefully, because it must reflect what the destination host can handle and the normal delay of relaying.
sections.plainLanguage: Each post office along the way passes the deadline on, but with the time that is left. If a post office cannot understand deadlines, a 'send it back' package is not allowed to go through it.

sections.title: Delivery Status Notification Changes
sections.content:
DSNs generated for a Deliver By request should include the optional Arrival-Date field, and this RFC adds a new per-message field to the DSN format of RFC 1894, Deliver-by-date. It carries the deliver-by-time as computed by the server that generates the DSN, written as an RFC 822 date-time as amended by RFC 1123.

The RFC therefore updates RFC 1894.
sections.plainLanguage: The note that comes back now has an extra line saying which deadline the post office was working toward.

sections.title: Security and Other Considerations
sections.content:
Deliver By makes it easier to trace a mail transport system. The trace letter T asks for a trace explicitly. Even without it, a crude trace can be built by sending a series of messages with growing by-time values such as BY=0;R, BY=1;R, BY=2;R. The RFC notes that probing can be done by other means too, such as looking at Received: header lines in bounced messages or using traceroute.

Servers are not required to give Deliver By messages or their DSNs any special priority. Even with BY=60;R, the sender is not guaranteed to learn of a failure within any particular time, because the DSN is not necessarily sped back to the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the deadline makes each stop report what happened, a nosy person could use it to map the route mail takes. And the post office still does not promise to hurry.
